deep.reconstruction:
OVERALL: The page finds solutions of the 3-D Laplace equation of the form u(x,r)cos(nψ), and transforms the meridian-plane equation into bipolar (toroidal) coordinates. This is the geometry of a ring (anchor ring/torus). The right half of the page is the derivation; the left half is the attempted solution by Fourier and power series. The previous and next pages contain the companion integral representations: (1-ρe^{iθ})^n expansions and ∫f(r cosθ + x i) cos nθ dθ.

RIGHT HALF (derivation of the PDE).
(R1) Coordinates are x, y, z with y = r cosψ and z = r sinψ. Then u_yy + u_zz = (1/r)(r u_r)_r + (1/r²)u_ψψ, so Δu = u_xx + (1/r)(r u_r)_r + (1/r²)u_ψψ = 0. Taking u ∝ cos nψ (or e^{inψ}) gives the meridian equation
  u_xx + (1/r)(r u_r)_r − (n²/r²) u = 0.
(R2) Complex characteristic variables: z = r + x i and z' = r − x i, so 2r = z + z' and 2xi = z − z'. Then u_r = u_z + u_{z'} and u_x = i(u_z − u_{z'}). The manuscript's line labelled ∂u/∂r is really ∂u/∂x. Hence u_xx = −u_zz + 2u_zz' − u_z'z', and u_rr + u_xx = 4u_zz'. The equation becomes
  4 u_{zz'} + (2/(z+z'))(u_z + u_{z'}) − (4n²/(z+z')²) u = 0.
This is a complex Euler–Poisson–Darboux-type equation.
(R3) Möbius map to bipolar coordinates. Riemann writes (a+z)/(a−z) = ρe^{iφ} and solves for z = a(ρe^{iφ}−1)/(ρe^{iφ}+1). He then normalizes a = 1: y = (1+z)/(1−z) and y' = (1+z')/(1−z'). Consequences:
  z = (y−1)/(y+1) = 1 − 2/(y+1),
  dz = 2dy/(y+1)²,
  z + z' = 2(yy'−1)/((y+1)(y'+1)).
Substituting gives u_z = ½(y+1)² u_y and 4u_{zz'} = (y+1)²(y'+1)² u_{yy'}. After dividing out, the equation is
  u_{yy'} + (1/(yy'−1))·½[u_y (y+1)/(y'+1) + u_{y'} (y'+1)/(y+1)] − n²u/(yy'−1)² = 0.
(R4) Polar form: y = ρe^{iφ} and y' = ρe^{−iφ}. Then log y = log ρ + iφ and log y' = log ρ − iφ, so 2 log ρ = log y + log y' and 2iφ = log y − log y'. It follows that
  ∂/∂log y = ½∂/∂logρ − (i/2)∂/∂φ (the manuscript has +i/2),
  u_{log y log y'} = ¼(u_{LL} + u_φφ), with L = log ρ.
Multiply the equation by yy'(y+1)(y'+1)/ρ, using
  (y+1)(y'+1) = ρ(ρ + 1/ρ + 2cosφ),
  yy' − 1 = ρ(ρ − 1/ρ),
  (y+1)²/y = 2 + y + 1/y,
  y + 1/y = (ρ+1/ρ)cosφ + i(ρ−1/ρ)sinφ.
The bottom-right lines are these auxiliary computations. The result is the first line of the page:
  ¼(u_LL + u_φφ)(ρ+1/ρ+2cosφ) + (1/(ρ−1/ρ))[½u_L(2 + (ρ+1/ρ)cosφ) + ½(ρ−1/ρ)u_φ sinφ] − n²u(ρ+1/ρ+2cosφ)/(ρ−1/ρ)² = 0.
With ρ = e^η, one has r = sinh η/(cosh η + cos φ) and x = sin φ/(cosh η + cos φ). These are exactly toroidal coordinates, with φ shifted by π. Riemann's attempt at r = .../(√(1+y²) + cos φ) is a version of this.

LEFT HALF (attempted solution).
(L1) Expansion u = Σ a_m(ρ) cos mφ. Because the equation contains the factors (ρ+1/ρ+2cosφ) and sinφ·u_φ, each a_m couples to a_{m−1}, a_m and a_{m+1}. That is the meaning of the line 'a_{m−1}cos(m−1)φ + a_m cos mφ + a_{m+1}cos(m+1)φ'.
(L2) Riemann writes the contribution of a_m to the cos(m+1)φ coefficient. Equivalently, it is the e^{i(m+1)φ} component for the ansatz a(ρ)e^{imφ}:
  ¼(a_LL − m²a) + ¼ a_L(ρ+1/ρ)/(ρ−1/ρ) + ¼ m a − n²a/(ρ−1/ρ)².
I checked this coefficient; it is correct. With ω = ρ − 1/ρ one has dω = (ρ+1/ρ)dL. Therefore (1/ω)(ω a_L)_L = a_LL + ((ρ+1/ρ)/ω)a_L. So the expression equals ¼[(1/ω)(ω a_L)_L − m(m−1)a − 4n²a/ω²]. Riemann rewrites this as ∂(ω ∂a/∂L)/(ω∂L) ± 4n²a − m(m−1)aω², i.e. multiplied through by ω².
(L3) Auxiliary ODE: ∂/∂L = (ρ+1/ρ)∂/∂ω and (ρ+1/ρ)² = ω² + 4. Hence ∂²/∂L² = (ω²+4)∂²_ω + ω∂_ω. Setting this minus n² equal to zero gives (ω²+4)s'' + ωs' − n²s = 0, whose solutions are ρ^{±n}.
(L4) Power series a_m = Σ s_ν ω^ν. Substitution gives
  Σ ω^{ν+2}(ν²+ν−m(m−1))s_ν + Σ ω^ν(4ν² − 4n²)s_ν = 0.
Riemann notes ν²+ν−m²+m = (ν−m+1)(ν+m). Shifting the index gives the two-term recurrence
  (ν−1−m)(ν−2+m)s_{ν−2} ± 4(ν−n)(ν+n)s_ν = 0.
The correct sign is +; the manuscript has −. The indicial roots are ν = ±n.
(L5) Riemann then tries to solve the recurrence with Gauss's Π-function (Π(x) = Γ(x+1)): s_{2ν} involves Π(ν − (n+m)/2)…/Π(ν − n/2)Π(ν + n/2). He sums via an Euler beta-integral, ∫_0^1 (1−x)^{(n−1+m)/2…} x^{(n+m−1)/2…} (1 − (ω/2)²x)^{…} dx. My completion: a_m = ω^n·₂F₁((n−1−m)/2, (n+m−2)/2; n+1; −ω²/4), which with Riemann's sign would have argument +ω²/4. The fragments ∂ω/∂s and (∂u/∂s)(∂s/∂ω) are unfinished change-of-variable notes.
errors: The line transcribed as ∂u/∂r = i∂u/∂z − i∂u/∂z' is correct only as ∂u/∂x. The next line, u_xx = −u_zz + 2u_zz' − u_z'z', confirms that x is meant.

Sign slip: ∂u/∂log y = ½∂u/∂logρ − (i/2)∂u/∂φ, not + (i/2). It does not affect the product formula u_{log y log y'} = ¼(u_LL + u_φφ). The final (ρ,φ) equation on the page has the correct sign of the sinφ·u_φ term.

Recurrence sign: from Σω^{ν+2}(ν²+ν−m(m−1))s_ν + Σω^ν(4ν²−4n²)s_ν = 0 one gets (ν−1−m)(ν−2+m)s_{ν−2} + 4(ν−n)(ν+n)s_ν = 0. The manuscript writes −4(…). This flips the hypergeometric argument from −ω²/4 to +ω²/4 in the Euler-integral attempt.
In the rewritten coefficient equation the 4nn a_m term should carry a minus sign, i.e. ω²(1/ω)(ωa_L)_L − 4n²a − m(m−1)ω²a; the sign as written looks inconsistent.

Methodological gap: the PDE in toroidal coordinates is not separable as written; it is only R-separable after u = √(coshη + cosφ)·v. Isolating the single coupling coefficient of a_m in cos(m+1)φ does not by itself yield a solution of the coupled three-term system. The e^{imφ}, e^{i(m±1)φ} components impose three different ODEs on one function, so this is exploratory.
The Π/integral lines at the lower left are fragmentary and partly crossed out; exponents of the Euler integral cannot be confirmed.

results.what: Reduction of 3-D Laplace with cos nψ dependence to the meridian equation u_xx + (1/r)(r u_r)_r − n²u/r² = 0
results.modern_name: Separation in cylindrical coordinates / axisymmetric potential theory

results.what: Characteristic complex variables z = r + ix, z' = r − ix giving 4u_zz' + 2(u_z+u_z')/(z+z') − 4n²u/(z+z')² = 0
results.modern_name: Complex Euler–Poisson–Darboux form of the axisymmetric (Weinstein/GASPT) equation
results.usually_credited_to: Euler, Poisson, Darboux; Riemann's own 1860 method for hyperbolic equations is related

results.what: Möbius map (1+z)/(1−z) = ρe^{iφ} turning the meridian plane into bipolar coordinates, i.e. 3-D toroidal coordinates r = sinhη/(coshη+cosφ), x = sinφ/(coshη+cosφ), and the transformed Laplace equation
results.modern_name: Toroidal coordinates; Laplace equation for toroidal harmonics (ring functions)
results.usually_credited_to: C. Neumann (1864, 'Theorie der Elektricitäts- und Wärme-Vertheilung in einem Ringe'); W. M. Hicks (1881)

results.what: Fourier expansion in φ producing three-term coupling, with a power-series and recurrence ansatz in ω = ρ − 1/ρ
results.modern_name: Frobenius method / hypergeometric series for (Legendre-type) toroidal functions
results.usually_credited_to: Frobenius-type series (Euler, Gauss); toroidal functions: Neumann, Hicks

results.what: Summation of the series via an Euler beta-integral with Gauss Π-function
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (1769), Gauss (1812); used extensively by Riemann (1857)

deep.surprise_reason: Each technique is standard for Riemann: characteristic complex variables, the Π-function, hypergeometric series, Euler integrals and potential theory. The notable point is the explicit use of toroidal coordinates for Laplace's equation, via a Möbius/bipolar map in the meridian plane. If the page predates 1864, this anticipates C. Neumann's ring-function theory, plausibly linked to Riemann's work on Nobili rings and electrostatics. However, the computation is unfinished and contains sign slips, and the dating is uncertain. So it is a notable unpublished detail rather than a major priority claim.

transcription_corrections: '∂u/∂r = ∂u/∂z i − ∂u/∂z' i' should read ∂u/∂x = i∂u/∂z − i∂u/∂z'.
The z,z' equation should end '= 0' (with a = 1 normalization noted), not '= −1'.
The middle term of the y,y' equation carries a factor ½: (1/(yy'−1))·½(∂u/∂y·(y+1)/(y'+1) + ∂u/∂y'·(y'+1)/(y+1)).
'∂a_m/(ρ∂logρ)' is better read as ∂a_m/∂logρ = Σ ν s_ν (ρ−1/ρ)^{ν−1}(ρ+1/ρ).
'r = …/(√(1+y²)+cosφ)' is a fragment of r = (ρ−1/ρ)/(ρ+1/ρ+2cosφ), i.e. sinhη/(coshη+cosφ); the √(1+y²) there denotes coshη with y = sinhη.
The trailing-term factor in the first equation is (ρ+1/ρ+2cosφ) multiplying −n²u/(ρ−1/ρ)²; this reading is confirmed.
